title: Very Fast Bayesian Additive Regression Trees on GPU
claim: A tree model is a hierarchy of threshold rules that partitions the input space into regions, each with a constant prediction.
layout: 2 panels, left tree diagram and right partition, red callout labels
description: The figure has two panels. On the left is a small binary decision tree. The root box reads x1 < 0.8 and has YES and NO branches. The NO branch goes to a green leaf circle, μ3. The YES branch goes to an internal box reading x2 < 0.4, which has YES and NO branches to a blue leaf μ1 and an orange leaf μ2. Red text labels with arrows name each part: Root, Internal node, Decision rule, Splitting axis, Splitting point (cutpoint), Leaf, and Leaf value. On the right is the matching partition of the unit square, with x1 on the horizontal axis and x2 on the vertical axis. A vertical line at 0.8 and a horizontal line at 0.4 split it into three rectangles. The rectangles use the same colors as the leaves (blue μ1, orange μ2, green μ3). The red annotations draw the eye first.
caption: Depiction and terminology of a decision tree. Adapted from [ref].
abstract: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) is a nonparametric Bayesian regression technique based on an ensemble of decision trees. It is part of the toolbox of many statisticians. The overall statistical quality of the regression is typically higher than other generic alternatives, and it requires less manual tuning, making it a good default choice. However, it is a niche method compared to natural competitors such as XGBoost, due to the longer running time, making sample sizes above 10000-100000 a nuisance. We present a GPU implementation of BART, up to 500x faster than the previous state of the art, making BART fast enough to be a viable option on large datasets, and showing that BART parallelizes better than its non-Bayesian counterparts. We also find that, to be as practical as tree boosting on large datasets, BART would need a scalable way to infer the number of trees, which we do not provide. Our implementation is available in the Python package bartz.
